passage: Ramesh woke in the dark of their Nagpur flat and saw a tall shape with long arms on the wall. He pulled the sheet over his head and yelled for Nana. Rafiq came in and switched on the light. "Look, beta. What's there?" Ramesh peeked. It was Nana's raincoat on the hook, with the street light behind it. Rafiq switched the light off and made a rabbit shadow with his hands. Ramesh giggled and made a dog. "Can the small lamp stay on?" "Of course," said Rafiq, and sat with him until he slept.

qa.q: What was the tall shape on the wall really?
qa.a: It was Nana's raincoat on the hook, with the street light behind it.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh pull the sheet over his head?
qa.a: He was frightened because he imagined the shadow was a monster.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that helped Ramesh with his fear?
qa.a: He showed him the real cause, turned it into a shadow game, kept the small lamp on and stayed with him.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel being woken in the night?
qa.a: He may be sleepy, but he stays patient because he wants Ramesh to feel safe.

grounding: It shows a child separating an imagined monster from reality and accepting comfort.

passage:
"Papa! There's a monster under my bed!"
Kishore came in with the torch. "Shall we look together?"
Reena clutched his kurta. "You look first."
He shone the torch. "One slipper. One lost crayon. Lots of dust."
"No monster?"
"No monster. Monsters are pretend. But the scared feeling is real, hmm?"
Reena nodded. "It's big."
"Then let's hug it smaller." He held her tight.
"Can the torch sleep next to me?"
"Yes."

qa.q: What did Kishore find under the bed?
qa.a: One slipper, one lost crayon and lots of dust.

qa.q: What does Reena clutching his kurta and saying "You look first" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was still scared and needed Papa close to feel brave enough to check.

qa.q: Which part of Kishore's response was wise?
qa.a: He looked with her, said monsters are pretend, but still took her feeling seriously and comforted her.

qa.q: What would change if Kishore had laughed at the fear?
qa.a: Reena might hide her fears next time and feel alone with them instead of accepting comfort.

grounding: It shows a child separating imagined monsters from reality with a parent's comfort.

passage:
Nursery note, nap time. Written by Vandana, teacher.
The power went off during nap and the room went dark. Harsha (5) sat up and whispered, "There's a ghost in the cupboard." I opened the cupboard with my phone light: mops and a bucket. He held my hand for a while. Later I heard him tell a friend, "It was only mops." 🙂
Next: I'll keep a small torch in the nap room and let the children check corners with it.

qa.q: What was in the cupboard?
qa.a: There were mops and a bucket in the cupboard.

qa.q: What does Harsha holding Vandana's hand suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he still felt a little scared and wanted comfort even after seeing the cupboard.

qa.q: How does Vandana plan to help the children with the dark?
qa.a: Vandana plans to keep a small torch in the nap room and let children check corners themselves.

qa.q: How might Harsha's friend be affected by hearing "It was only mops"?
qa.a: The friend may feel less scared of the dark too, hearing it from another child.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child separating an imagined ghost from reality and accepting comfort.

passage:
The power went out in their village house near Kolhapur, and Madhav, five, sat up on his mat. In the corner stood a tall, lumpy shape with long arms.

"Aai! A monster!" he whispered.

Vandana lit the lantern and held it up. "Let's look together."

The shape was the grain sack with Baba's coat hung over it, sleeves dangling.

Madhav stared. "It looked real."

"In the dark, things play tricks," she said, stroking his hair. He lay down, but kept one hand on her sari.

qa.q: What was the lumpy shape in the corner really?
qa.a: It was the grain sack with Baba's coat hung over it.

qa.q: How can you tell Madhav still felt a little uneasy after the lantern was lit?
qa.a: He lay down but kept one hand on his mother's sari, still wanting her closeness.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that helped Madhav separate imagination from reality?
qa.a: She lit the lantern and looked with him, so he could see for himself what the shape was, and then comforted him.

qa.q: What would change if Vandana had laughed at Madhav's fear?
qa.a: He might feel ashamed and hide his fears next time, instead of accepting her comfort.

grounding: Shows a young child in a village facing an imagined monster in the dark and accepting comfort.

passage:
"There's something under my bed," Tariq, five, called from his room in their Amman flat.

His sister Dalia came in with a torch. "What does it look like?"

"Big teeth. It growls."

"Let's check. You hold the torch."

Tariq pointed the light under the bed. Two socks, a toy truck, and a ball.

"The growl?" she asked. Outside, the neighbour's water pump rumbled.

Tariq giggled. "It's the pump!" He took the torch to bed with him, just in case.

qa.q: What was under the bed when Tariq pointed the torch?
qa.a: There were two socks, a toy truck and a ball.

qa.q: Why did Tariq take the torch to bed with him?
qa.a: He felt better but still a little unsure, so keeping the torch made him feel safe.

qa.q: What worked well in how Dalia helped?
qa.a: She let Tariq hold the torch and check himself, so he discovered that the monster and growl were imaginary.

qa.q: How might Dalia feel about being called for monsters?
qa.a: She seems patient and caring, taking his fear seriously enough to help.

grounding: Shows a young child abroad checking an imagined monster with a sibling's help and accepting comfort.

passage:
At nap time in the crèche, the curtains were drawn and the room was dim. Deepak, five, sat up suddenly and pointed.
“Ganga-didi! A monster by the door!”
Ganga tiptoed over and switched on the small lamp. On the hook hung a long black raincoat with a hood.
“Look, it's Mr Das's raincoat,” she whispered. “Want to touch it?”
Deepak touched the sleeve. “It's just a coat.”
“Just a coat. Shall I leave the lamp on?”
He nodded, lay down and held her hand until his eyes closed.

qa.q: What was hanging on the hook?
qa.a: A long black raincoat with a hood.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when he saw the shape by the door?
qa.a: He felt frightened, thinking it was a monster.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that helped Deepak separate imagination from reality?
qa.a: She switched on the lamp and let him touch the coat so he could see and feel what it really was.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel when Deepak holds her hand and falls asleep?
qa.a: She likely feels tender and relieved that he feels safe again.

grounding: A crèche helper helps a five-year-old see that an imagined monster is only a coat, and comforts him.

passage:
I'm Nitin, Dilnaz's uncle. On Saturday I was babysitting, and at bedtime Dilnaz, five, screamed. “Chachu! There's a wolf on the wall!”
It was the shadow of the window grille and a plant, stretched by the street light.
I sat on her bed and made a shadow with my hands: a dog. Then a bird. Then a wolf.
“It's your hands!” she said.
“And the one on the wall?”
She looked. “It's the plant.” Then she made her own wobbly bird.
I don't know if she really believed me. But she fell asleep.

qa.q: What made the shadow on the wall?
qa.a: The window grille and a plant, stretched by the street light.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when she saw the wolf shadow?
qa.a: She felt scared, screaming for her uncle.

qa.q: How did the hand-shadow game help Dilnaz?
qa.a: It showed her how shadows are made, so she could see the wolf was only the plant.

qa.q: How does Nitin see his success?
qa.a: Nitin is unsure whether she fully believed him, but relieved that she fell asleep.

grounding: An uncle helps a five-year-old see that a scary shadow is not a real wolf.

passage:
Monday night: Gautam, five, wouldn't get into bed. “There's a monster under it.” His cousin Imran, fifteen, who shared the room, sat with him till he slept.
Tuesday night: Imran gave Gautam a torch. “Let's check together.” Under the bed they found shoes, a ball, and dust. “No monster,” said Imran. Gautam still slept with the torch.
Friday night: Gautam knelt down and shone the torch under the bed himself. “Just shoes,” he announced, and climbed in.

qa.q: What did they find under the bed on Tuesday?
qa.a: They found shoes, a ball and dust.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel on Friday when he checked under the bed?
qa.a: He felt brave and confident, announcing it was just shoes.

qa.q: Why did giving Gautam a torch help?
qa.a: It let him check for himself, so he could see there was nothing to fear.

qa.q: How might Imran feel on Friday night?
qa.a: Imran probably feels proud and relieved that Gautam can now check alone.

grounding: Over a week a five-year-old learns the monster under his bed is imaginary, with a cousin's comfort.

passage:
The storm knocked out the power at Nani's house, and the torch was missing. Ira lay stiff under the quilt. Lightning flashed. A tall figure stood in the corner with long arms.
"Didi," she whispered. "There's a monster."
Aadhya didi fumbled for her phone and switched on its light. "Where?"
Ira pointed. The light showed Nana's raincoat hanging on the hook, its sleeves dangling.
"Touch it," said Aadhya. Ira crept over and squeezed a wet sleeve. "It's just the raincoat."
She climbed back and let Aadhya hug her until the thunder faded.

qa.q: What was hanging on the hook?
qa.a: Nana's raincoat.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she lay stiff under the quilt?
qa.a: Ira was frightened; in the dark the raincoat looked like a monster to her.

qa.q: Which step helped Ira tell imagination from reality?
qa.a: Aadhya let Ira see and touch the raincoat herself, so Ira found out it was not a monster.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel during the storm?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel a bit tense herself with no power, but she stays calm to comfort Ira.

grounding: During a power cut a child checks a scary shape, finds it is a raincoat, and accepts a hug.

passage:
On a foggy December night in Delhi, Seema screamed. "Mumma! Something white is at the window!"
Himani came in and sat on the bed. "Show me."
Seema pointed at a pale shape floating outside, moving in the wind.
"Shall we look together?" Himani held her hand and drew the curtain back. It was Mrs Bedi's white shawl, drying on the next balcony.
Seema stared. "It looked like a ghost."
"In the dark, lots of things do."
Seema let Himani tuck her in, holding her hand a little longer.

qa.q: What was the white shape at the window?
qa.a: Mrs Bedi's white shawl, drying on the next balcony.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she said "It looked like a ghost"?
qa.a: Seema was still a little shaken but relieved to see it was only a shawl.

qa.q: What did Himani do that helped Seema?
qa.a: Himani didn't laugh; she looked together with Seema, so Seema could check the scary shape herself.

qa.q: What would change if Himani had said "Don't be silly, go to sleep"?
qa.a: Seema would probably stay scared and feel dismissed, without finding out what the shape really was.

grounding: On a foggy winter night a mother helps her child see that a scary shape is a shawl.

passage:
"Mumma, there's a monster under my bed. It growls."
Binita put down the lamp. "Growls? Like what?"
"Grrr, grrrr."
They listened. Rain drummed on the tin roof. The drainpipe gurgled. Grrr, grrrr.
"Hmm," said Binita. "What does the drainpipe sound like when it rains?"
Sahil listened again. "…Like that."
"Want to look under the bed with me?"
Sahil peeked with the lamp. Dust and one lost sock. "No monster."
"No monster. But you can still hold my hand."
Sahil held it and yawned.

qa.q: What did Sahil find under the bed?
qa.a: Dust and one lost sock.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he said the monster growls?
qa.a: Sahil was scared, because the drainpipe sound in the rain seemed like a growl to him.

qa.q: How did Binita help Sahil work it out himself?
qa.a: She asked what the drainpipe sounds like in rain and let him look under the bed, so he could see there was no monster.

qa.q: How might Binita feel when Sahil yawns and holds her hand?
qa.a: Binita probably feels relieved and tender 🤍, glad he is calm enough to sleep.

grounding: On a rainy night a child tests his fear of a growling monster and accepts comfort.

passage:
Parent's note to the preschool, winter
Disha (5) has been scared of the dark since the long winter nights began. She says a monster lives in the cupboard. Last night she screamed when the power went out.
Her older brother Tenzin sat with her and opened the cupboard with a torch. "See? Only sweaters."
Disha peeked, then laughed. "Monster is pretend."
We have put a small night light in her room. She hugged me and slept. Please let us know if she mentions it at school.

qa.a: In the cupboard.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when the power went out?
qa.a: She felt frightened, screaming in the dark.

qa.q: What helped Disha separate the monster from reality?
qa.a: Tenzin opening the cupboard with a torch to show only sweaters, and a night light.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel after helping his sister?
qa.a: Tenzin likely feels proud and caring, glad she laughed.

grounding: A parent's note shows a young child learning a monster is pretend and accepting comfort.

passage:
On a hot summer night in their village, Nitin, five, refused to sleep on the roof with the family. "There's a ghost in the neem tree!"
His grandfather Thomas lay beside him and pointed. "That's the wind moving the leaves. Listen."
Nitin listened. Rustle, rustle.
"And the white thing?"
"The moon on the branch."
Nitin held Thomas's hand tight, watching the tree. Slowly his grip loosened. He fell asleep counting stars.

qa.q: What did Nitin think was in the neem tree?
qa.a: A ghost.

qa.q: How was Nitin feeling at first?
qa.a: He felt scared, refusing to sleep on the roof.

qa.q: How did Thomas help Nitin?
qa.a: He lay beside him and explained what the sounds and shapes really were.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel as Nitin's grip loosens?
qa.a: Thomas probably feels relieved and tender.

grounding: Shows a young child separating imagined ghosts from reality with a grandparent's comfort.

passage:
On a stormy autumn night in Lagos, Emeka, five, called out, "Mummy! There's a monster at the window!"
His mother Yara came with a lamp. Thunder rolled. A branch scratched the glass.
"Look," she said, lifting the curtain. "It's the mango branch."
Emeka peeked. "But it has fingers."
"Leaves. Want to touch it tomorrow?"
He nodded, snuggling into her. "Stay till I sleep?"
She stayed.

qa.q: What was scratching the glass?
qa.a: A branch, the mango branch.

qa.q: How did Emeka feel during the storm?
qa.a: He felt afraid, calling out that there was a monster.

qa.q: What did Yara do that helped?
qa.a: She showed him the real branch, offered to touch it tomorrow, and stayed till he slept.

qa.q: How might Yara feel staying with Emeka?
qa.a: Yara likely feels patient and loving.

grounding: Shows a young child learning a scary shape is real and ordinary, and accepting comfort.

passage:
A monsoon storm knocked out the power during nap time at the Pune daycare. The room went grey. Payal, five, sat bolt upright and pointed at the corner. "A monster! With a long arm!"
Chetan Sir came over with a torch. "Shall we look together?"
Payal held his sleeve. He shone the torch. It was Rhea's raincoat hanging on a hook, one sleeve dangling.
"It's a coat," Payal whispered. "But it looked real."
"Our eyes play tricks in the dark," Chetan Sir said. "Want the torch next to your mat?"
Payal nodded, lay down, and kept one hand on it.

qa.q: What was really in the corner?
qa.a: It was Rhea's raincoat hanging on a hook, one sleeve dangling.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she sat bolt upright?
qa.a: She felt frightened, sure she was seeing a monster with a long arm.

qa.q: What went well in the way Chetan Sir handled the fear?
qa.a: He didn't laugh at her; he looked with her, showed her it was a coat, and let her keep the torch for comfort.

qa.q: What would change if Chetan Sir had just told Payal to go back to sleep?
qa.a: Payal might have stayed scared and not learned that the monster was only a coat in the dark.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to tell imagination from reality and accepting comfort from an adult.
